title: Valerian
subtitle: The classic sleep herb: dried root for infusions, tinctures, and baths
excerpt: Valerian is the most widely used sleep herb in western herbal practice. The dried root makes a strong-smelling infusion or tincture taken in the evening for difficulty falling asleep and physical tension. A tin of dried root keeps 12 months in a cool dark cupboard.

glossaryTerms.definition: A herb traditionally used to support the nervous system, calming tension, easing anxiety, or improving sleep.
A preparation made by simmering harder plant material, roots, bark, seeds, in water and straining the liquid.
A concentrated herbal extract made by macerating dried or fresh herb in alcohol and water, then straining.

content.text: Valerian in the home medicine cupboard, dried root for infusions,
decoctions

, and baths taken in the evening. The most widely used sleep herb in western herbal practice, long prepared for difficulty settling, restlessness at night, and physical tension carried in the muscles. A tin of dried root keeps 12 months in a cool dark cupboard and makes 30 to 40 evening doses.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body: Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor before use. Full precautions are in the 'When not to use' section.

content.text: Botanical

Valeriana officinalis, family Caprifoliaceae (formerly Valerianaceae). A tall perennial, 1,1.5 m, with pinnate leaves and small clusters of pale pink-white flowers from late spring into summer. Found wild in damp meadows, stream banks, and disturbed ground across Europe and temperate Asia. widely naturalised in North America. The part used is the root and rhizome, harvested in autumn of the second year when the root system is mature. Fresh root has a mild smell. dried root develops the characteristic strong, musty odour as the valepotriates break down during drying.

Look-alikes: valerian is occasionally confused with common hogweed in the leaf, which can cause phototoxic skin burns on contact. Confirm root identity before harvest. Use cultivated dried root from a reputable supplier if in any doubt.
active compounds and actions
The root contains valepotriates (iridoid compounds), valeric acid, isovaleric acid, and flavonoids. These are the groups that western herbalists and researchers have focused on when studying the
nervine
action. Valepotriates are unstable and break down during drying. Modern research focuses on isovaleric acid and flavonoids as the active compounds in dried root.
Traditional uses

Western herbal tradition records valerian for restlessness and difficulty sleeping. This covers the kind of sleeplessness linked to an overactive mind or tension at night. The 20th-century herbalist Grieve gives guidance on preparing the dried root. Current herbal guidance supports traditional use for mild nervous tension and short-term sleep problems.
Preparations

Infusion (herbal brew method): 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried root per 200 ml water, cold-start, bring to gentle simmer for 10 minutes, steep covered a further 10 minutes. The taste is strong, bitter, and musty. many people add honey and a little peppermint to make it palatable.

Herbal extract (dried herb, 1:5 in 40% spirit): the standard western herbal preparation for reliable dosing. Macerates 4 to 6 weeks, strains to a dark bottle. Dose: 3 to 5 ml in a little water, taken 30 to 60 minutes before bed. The
tincture
is the more palatable and better-absorbed preparation. the infusion is traditional but variable in strength.
Bath: 50 g dried root steeped in 1 litre of water for 20 minutes, strained, added to a warm bath. For physical tension rather than oral dosing. Some systemic absorption through skin is possible.
Cautions and reasons to avoid

Drug interactions: valerian adds to the sedating effect of many medications. These include sleeping tablets, opioids, and sedating antihistamines. Alcohol also adds to the effect. Do not take valerian alongside any of these.
Pregnancy: do not use valerian. Current safety guidance does not support it, due to limited safety data. Consult a herbalist or midwife if you are unsure.
Driving: Valerian may affect reaction times and alertness. Do not drive or operate machinery for several hours after taking valerian until you know how it affects you.

Long-term use: The traditional western herbal literature is comfortable with valerian taken for weeks at a time for sleep problems. The European herbal guidance reference entry covers short-term use (up to 4 weeks). For longer courses, the involvement of a herbalist is appropriate.
